Thanks for pointing out the Electronic Visualization Center document from January 1980 that includes the monitor circuit on archive.org, Kevin.  I have a scan of that from the Vasulka archive:

http://www.vasulka.org/archive/sitemap.html

It's good to see that they're adding it to archive.org.  It was rather obscure to find it before now.

Phil Morton was a digital artist.  He died quite young, I think, in the 1980s or early 1990s.  There is a video with Jane Veeder on YouTube where she talks about him (which I can't find right now).

Dan Sandin invented the Image Processor in 1973.  He also worked with Tom DeFanti, who has his own ties to the Bally Arcade (namely, ZGRASS).  Dan has his own Wikipedia page:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_J._Sandin

You can read about them Phil and Dan in this 1985 document, here:

https://ballyalley.com/documentation/zgrass/zgrass-uv-1_articles/Chicago%20Biographies%20of%20Interactive%20Life-style/Chicago%20Biographies%20of%20Interactive%20Life-style.pdf

Of course, you can probably use Google and find a TON of material about Sandin.  He's quite famous in certain circles.

Also, search BallyAlley.com for both of their names.  In particular, you'll find some letters about or written to Phil here:

https://ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/letters/letters.html

Again, thanks for pointing out that document, Kevin.  How did you bump into it?

Adam

19003:
I thought that I had added Dan Sandin's video circuit to BallyAlley, but I couldn't find it when I looked for it a couple of hours ago.  It turns out I added it on August 16, 2019.  Here is the link:

https://ballyalley.com/documentation/misc_hardware_docs/misc_hardware_docs.html#CompositeVideoforAstrocadePhilMorton

Here are the notes I posted about it at the time:

-----

Composite Video Modification for the Bally Arcade/Astrocade.
By Dan Sandin and Phil Morton of the Electronic Visualization Center.
1980.

This is an add-on circuit which improves the audio and video signals, optimizing for recording and/or transmission. This add-on circuit gives the computer user a line level audio signal output and a composite video signal output. It is a lowest-possible-cost solution to a highest-possible-quality goal.

This add-on circuit was-designed and prototyped by Dan Sandin; copied and documented by Phil Morton. The document includes instructions, schematic, board layout and parts list.

The circuit diagram and 2X printed circuit board pictorial can be directly copied by Sandin IMAGE PROCESSOR builders using parts already on hand. The circuit is a slight variation on the "standard driver" used so frequently through-out the Sandin IMAGE PROCESSOR.

On August 16, 2019, "maginnovision" on the Yahoo group (in message #16486) noted that this project "might work in conjunction with the RF modulator. If the RF isn't there you get 0 color. If you use the RF it's not much different than [Ken Lill's] circuit. I'd argue the board I suggested will give better results [...] however it isn't as easy for some people to use as you either need a PCB printed or solder it [using dead bug prototyping]. The recommended circuit also isn't properly terminated for composite. It uses 47 ohm as opposed to 75 ohm."

-----

I'm glad that I'm not completely bonkers about what I've placed on BallyAlley in the past.  This is another example of how difficult it is to find material on that site of mine.  Ugh.

Adam

19005:
There have been quite a few video upgrades for the Astrocade over the years.  Matt's project sounds interesting, as it might (?) use component.  The other upgrades have been s-video and composite upgrades.  I've used both, but I stick with RF-out, as my experience with the others has always been faded colors, bleeding or ghosting.

My Astrocade's RF-out is fuzzy with my 14" Toshiba, but-- heck!-- it probably looks better using my "modern" flatscreen CRT from about fifteen years ago than it looked on the newest CRT in 1978.

On a semi-related note, I have been using my Timex/Sinclair 2068 nearly every day recently and it has the worst RF-out ever.  "Luckily," it also has composite-out, which is just as bad or worse than its RF-out.  This is a known issue and therefore I use a digital RGB adapter with an HDMI adapter to get a crystal-clear picture on an inexpensive 12" HDMI monitor.  However, digital RGB only offers eight colors, so I lose the additional "brite" colors that are output via RF and composite on the T/S 2068 computer.

Adam

19035:
Report 3 - Because there are a few Astrocade enthusiasts curious about my final modified for hi-res Astrocade project, I thought it would be appropriate to post the following on the Astrocade discussion group site.

Adam Trionfo added his commentary to MCMs YouTube channel video entitled: MCMs Final Hi-Res Astrocade - Report 1.

Within his commentary, Adam inquired about the hi-res Astrocade's:
add-under Pattern Transfer Board 3 and
a possible modified Cartridge Connector Interface (CCI).

Adam also inquired about a major motherboard schematic error in the Bally PA-1 Service Manual.

THE PATTERN TRANSFER BOARD 3 (PTB3)

The PTB3 scheme will be taken from the coin-op Wizard Of Wor PTB scheme. MCM has already spent time on a feasibility study of the WOW PTB scheme and determined that this scheme is compatible with MCMs modified for hi-res Astrocade.

The WOW PTB functions like a digital logic graphics subroutine. Even though the board utilizes some slow CMOS chips, overall, the PTB graphics subroutine can execute faster than a similar subroutine in memory processed by a Z80 CPU operating with a 1.78 MHz system clock.

The PTB does not have to spend time fetching any Z80 instructions from memory. The PTB executes the graphics subroutine using digital logic gates.

The Z80 has to fetch an instruction from memory before it can execute it. The fetch time delay can take 4 or more system clock cycles, depending on how many bytes of Z80 machine code an instruction utilizes.

So, for the Astrocade's Z80 system clock of 1.78 MHz (560 nsec per cycle), there will be at least a 4 x 560 nsec delay just to fetch and instruction from memory.

This fetch delay will add up when the Z80 executes a subroutine because every instruction executed within the sub has to be fetched in order for the Z80 to process the entire subroutine.

The PTB3 project will be very time consuming. The scheme has to be breadboarded, tested and wire wrapped. MCM will have to determine specifically how the PTB scheme manipulates each graphic byte written to screen RAM for each of the 6 possible graphic write modes available.

There is just minimal programming documentation for the WOW PTB. MCM will likely have to create graphic machine language programs during the testing phase to completely understand how the PTB can manipulate graphic bytes. It is not clear at this time if the PTB can utilize the custom address and data chip's magic functions.

Why is MCM willing to spend an enormous amount of time to create the Pattern Transfer Board 3? Simply, because the possibility of having a fast PTB on a modified for hi-res Astrocade "is there" and could open the door to graphics manipulation never seen on an Astrocade. Combining that possibility with a multi-page (scene) option and up to 32KB available for a directly accessible program, addressed at 8000 - FFFFH, could provide the potential for some really awesome graphic games. The PTB challenge is there and MCM wants to attempt it.

Two other ideas relating to the PTB3 are on MCMs table.

1. Break down the WOW machine coding for its "attract" mode to see how the WOW PTB was utilized?
Program a close variation, as a hi-res demo, of that attract mode for execution on MCMs hi-res Astrocade?
MCM is not planning to break down WOW's "play mode" because MCM will convert the Astrocade's "The Incredible Wizard" to hi-res.

2. Create an upgraded variation of the PTB providing additional (extended) graphic manipulation?

THE MODIFIED CARTRIDGE CONNECTOR INTERFACE (CCI)

Another idea that is on MCMs table is the modified CCI. This interface scheme exists only on paper at this time. The modified interface is NOT related to the Astrobasic cartridge built-in audio interface.

The interface would require a minor rewire of the motherboard CC decoder. Some of the wiring would be connected to 2 DPDT mini-toggle switches mounted on the right side of the motherboard with the toggles protruding through the bottom of the Astrocade console.

With the 2 toggles in position 1, the CCI would be decoded normally at 2000 - 3FFFH. With the 2 toggles in position 2, the CCI would be decoded to function at 8000 - FFFFH.

There are enough contacts in the cartridge connector to run a 32KB EEPROM (or EPROM). A cartridge PC board would need a rewire to accommodate the 32KB chip. There would likely be a need for the bottom of the cartridge to have a gnd contact which would make contact with a gnd contact on the bottom of the floor of the cassette connector.

The intent of the modified CCI would be to optionally run 32KB cartridge programs at 8000 - FFFFH utilizing a 16KB hi-res BIOS at 0000 - 3FFFH. The hi-res BIOS, similar to the low-res BIOS, would be able to sense a cartridge at 8000H by checking for a cartridge sentinel at that address.

Larger than 32KB programs would be possible using more than 1 cartridge as long as the program allowed the user to insert another cartridge to continue the program. This possibility could be accomplished by loading/executing a loop program in screen RAM or including a standard loop program in the hi-res BIOS.

A MAJOR MOTHERBOARD SCHEMATIC ERROR IN THE BALLY PA-1 SERVICE MANUAL

This error was pointed to in the Bally schematic, documented and corrected within the Report 1 video indicated above at the video time interval 2:49 - 4:00. MCM has known about this error for years. The error is between the two U6 inverters gates, pin 4 to pin 1 and U20 pin 9.

The error correction is also documented on the Bally Alley. The correction appears in one of the handwritten scans within the BalcheckHR User Manual. The correction is in scan 9, The Bally/Astrocade Motherboard - Custom Address/Data.

Here's the link to the listing of handwritten scans for the BalcheckHR User Manual.

https://ballyalley.com/documentation/BallyCheck/BallyCheck.html#:~:text=BalcheckHR%20User%20Manual%20(Handwritten%20Scans)

End Of Report 3

19075:
Report 4 - Adam Trionfo provided another commentary for MCMs YouTube video entitled: MCMs Final Hi-Res Astrocade - Report 2

A portion of my reply to Adam is related to my final hi-res Astrocade along with some info related to troubleshooting the Astrocade motherboard. I decided to post my reply also on the Astrocade discussion group site.

This time I'm including Adam's commentary followed by my reply.

Thanks Adam for spending the time to write and post your commentary to my video. It's encouraging to receive some positive feedback from a viewer of one of my videos.

ADAM'S COMMENTARY

Hi-Res Report #2 - Comments

This video really gave me a warm feeling.  You manage to show that the Astrocade has the power to be more than it was when it shipped in 1978.  Your hi-res upgrade quadruples its resolution.  Plus, you show a diagnostic device called BalCheck that can help users track down hardware failures.  Here are a few additional comments.

- Once these two project boards were designed by you, how long did it take to wire-them-up so that each one worked perfectly?

- Creating a low-res-only breadboard as a diagnostic tool to help isolate a future hardware failure, or maybe even to simulate an error, is a great idea.

2:35 - This low-res-only breadboard set looks like a scheme that Doctor Frankenstein may have had in his laboratory; I mean this as a compliment.  Maybe you should add a Jacob's Ladder to your lab.  This arcing "toy" might not be healthy for your Astrocade's delicate health, but it will look cool.

- I forgot to switch the video resolution to 720p until quite a bit into viewing it.  Once I did that, then the quality was much-improved.

- The 6" fan used to circulate air across your Astrocade's motherboard and your prototype boards is a trick which I have used before when I have spent considerable time typing in a program or programming in BASIC.  Just a little bit of circulating air keeps the Astrocade surprisingly cool, but I don't suppose that this is a surprise to anyone.

- This hardware setup would have been the envy of the home computer club in the 1970s.  I wonder what Steve Wozniak would think of this Hi-Res Astrocade project.  Does he even know the Bally Arcade exists?  He was a 6502 fan himself; maybe he thinks that the Z80 CPU is rubbish.

- Watching BalCheck HR run on the TV while observing the 7-segment displays was a treat.  Thanks for sharing this hardware diagnostic tool with us.

- The Z80 Check Diagnostic Utility looks incredibly helpful.  Astrocade power-ups that give only a black screen when there is a hardware failure are incredibly common.  This black screen can be traced back to many different hardware failures.  Having the ability to easily check the function of the Z80 is probably a dramatic time saver.

- The hi-res breadboard has 16K of screen RAM on it, right?

- It was a good idea to simulate a RAM error to demonstrate the diagnostic capability of your BalCheckHR.

The error report for the bad RAM is:

0 4 I 2 0 H E L P.

This is clever.  It's amusing that the Astrocade is, essentially, asking for HELP.  Your breakdown of the error report displayed on the 7-segment display makes it clear how powerful this hardware diagnostic tool is for someone who is troubleshooting an Astrocade.  It's clear that it can really speed up the diagnostic process.

- With your "Remote ROM Program," you're able to disable the on-board ROM with, it seems, the flick of a switch.  This is an idea that is worth its weight in gold, for it seems like the failure of the 8K on-board ROM happens from time to time.  If that is the only failure of the motherboard, then this "Remote ROM" would be an easy way to figure out if that is the only failure of the Astrocade's hardware.

- Your explanation of your entire hardware setup is thorough and meticulous.  I was able to follow this hardware progress report with ease.

- I would absolutely love to see this hardware setup in person.

I enjoyed this video immensely.  I hope this progress report will give some aspiring Astrocade hackers a reason to create some of the projects that are available on ballyalley.com.

MCMs REPLY TO ADAM'S COMMENTARY

HOW LONG DID IT TAKE TO WIRE UP THOSE 2 PROJECT BOARDS SO EACH ONE WORKED PERFECTLY?

Creating a schematic for use with the Astrocade, breadboarding the scheme, testing and if necessary, tweaking the scheme so it functions perfect, takes many, many hours to complete. The larger the scheme, the more time is required. Then, the scheme has to be wire wrapped on a permanent board requiring even more time.

Patience and perseverance are usually necessary to complete a hardware add-on or upgrade project for the Astrocade.

What I normally do to stay focused and motivated, is look ahead, seeing in my mind the end result of my efforts.

USING A SMALL FAN TO KEEP HEATED MOTHERBOARD COMPONENTS COOL

I haven't decided yet if my final hi-res Astrocade will have an internal forced air fan to keep the heat generating components on the motherboard cooler. My decision will be made when I see how wide the add-under rack set up will be. There is likely not going to be enough room to mount the fan to force air up through the Astrocade console bottom and over the motherboard top. I might have to add some kind of baffle to redirect the air through the bottom of the Astrocade console.

Otherwise , I'll run the Astrocade with the console top off and my 6" fan placed behind the Astrocade to blow some air across the left side of the motherboard.

MCM DESIGN's UPGRADED BALCHECKHR DIAGNOSTIC BOARD

I upgraded the original BALCHECK 7-segment display decoder and its error display sequence. The original BALCHECK error display sequence could be hard to read at times. I know this because I did breadboard and run the original Balcheck scheme. The Bally Alley has the original Balcheck scheme and program code.

The upgraded decoder also allows the hex numbers A b C d E F to be displayed.

In the error code sequence, I added what looks like a capital I. It looks like this ][. I did this for 2 reasons.  When ][ is displayed, it indicates the data error INFO byte is displayed next. The other reason was to distinguish the scenario when the error code and the info byte are the same number.

For example 04 ][ 04 HE LP

Without the capital I present, the error sequence can be confusing to read. In my example, without the capital I present you would only see 04 HE LP flashing.

I made some other display changes. I did preserve most of the original Balcheck program. The additional changes that I made were to upgrade the original Balcheck so it would be a more useful diagnostic tool.

THE BLACK SCREEN POWER ON

I did some investigating and found out the custom address and data chips normally power on initializing the TV display as a black screen. A software program has to set up the four TV display parameters as desired.

Unfortunately, the ROM BIOS power up routine utilizes the ROM User Program Interface (UPI) to call 2 onboard subroutines to set up the TV display. The UPI and onboard subs utilize a Z80 stack area in the screen RAM when executed. If there is a motherboard failure relating to the screen RAM, the UPI will fail to execute and the TV display will remain black.

The motherboard custom chip TV display output ports may still function even if there is a failure in screen RAM or its interfacing. During a motherboard failure, using Z80 output instructions directly (not within a subroutine) to set up the TV display will INCREASE the chance of the TV display powering on with some kind of color or graphics, instead of a black screen.

This is why I won't use a subroutine to initialize the TV display in several of my Astrocade diagnostic programs. Perhaps the creator of the ROM BIOS was not concerned about any black screen power on and was simply trying to save a few bytes by setting up the TV display utilizing the UPI to call the onboard subs labeled SETOUT+1 (Sub#22) and COLSET+1 (Sub#24).

YOUR BREADBOARD 1 HAD 16KB OF SCREEN RAM RIGHT?

The hi-res breadboard 1 actually had 4 banks of 32KB SRAM, but the 3 address lines A12, A13 and A14 were grounded providing the needed 4 banks of 4KB RAM for hi-res.

MCM DESIGN's REMOTE ROM DIAGNOSTIC PROGRAM

The Remote ROM diagnostic program is useful as long as the motherboard ROM is functioning enough so it can be disabled. If the motherboard ROM is so bad that it's creating an issue with the operation of the Z80 address or data bus, then the Remote ROM program will also not execute.

End Of Reply

19115:
A cassette recorder that is eating tapes 9 times out of 10 is a very dirty mechanism that moves the tape along, the 3 main parts being the two spindles, and the third is the rubber "wheel" next to the head. All three of these are motor driven parts. The rubber wheel is motor driven both ways, the spindles are motor driven one way, one in reverse to rewind and one forward to play or fast forward. Only one is being driven at a time and the other is free moving in the opposite way from when it's motor driven.
If any one of these isn't moving as fast as the others it's because of being very dirty and this is when the tape gets "eaten" by the tape player. The 1 in 10 is mechanical failure, in that case something is usually jammed.

I of course was keeping a close eye on things so as soon as I saw one spindle not moving at the same speed as the other (the free spinning spindle) I knew the tape was not winding up on the other side, which means it's feeding into the machine someplace. If this is allowed to happen for more that a couple of seconds then the tape usually gets ruined and also usually tangles up the works. I caught it in time both times it ate a tape, and I was able to pull the tape out and wind it up with a pencil with no damage. I also use old tapes I don't care for, usually some genre or singer or band I don't like anyway. I often come across old tapes of all kinds in my maintenacnce side of the business hauling off "junk" for people. If they are still good, I reuse them to record what I want to them.

In this case, it was indeed a VERY dirty mechanism and after a good deep cleaning, It doesn't eat tapes anymore!

As to the volume issue, it turned out to be a loose wire on the sliding pot and after resoldering it, the volume worked. I now have a well cleaned, inside and out, fully functioning tape recorder with a brand new belt.

In any case, new pictures and descriptions of the process will be up on the blog by tomorrow sometime. This will be all at the very end of the blog.

MCMs REPLY

Adam, I think you were asking if the coin-op pattern transfer board (PTB) created the star twinkling effect. That's a really good question.

The PTB could have been used to initially write each star. A x,y coordinate randomizing routine was also likely used initially to write each star.

However, I have reason to believe the twinkling effect was generated by additional chips on the coin-op logic board not the PTB.

When you look at the logic board schematic, on the left there is a scheme with its output connected to the video line. On the input side of the scheme there are 4 input lines labeled as

STARS
SPKL 1
SPKL 2
SPKL 3

SPKL = Sparkle

These 4 input lines could likely be set (enabled?) by a single output port. According to the WOW disassembly on the Bally Alley, digital design trickery may have been utilized so these lines could be enabled by an input (not an output) to port 14H.

I just browsed the WOW logic board schematic. I did not dig deep into this scheme, but it looks like the WOWs PTB does NOT twinkle the stars or sparkle specific graphic patterns.

Some time ago, I asked myself the same question about the stars twinkling. This is why I'm thinking of breaking down the machine coding for WOWs "attract" mode because I could likely learn a lot about the PTBs application.

End of reply

10 PRINT "MY BALLY WORKS! ",

:INPUT

19150:
Matt said:

"one regulator (UA78GUIC) [for that I must replace in the Astrocade] cost me $35! And one transistor (I don't remember which between TIP31 and TIP137) cost $15!"

I had no idea that some of the components in the Bally Arcade are so rare now.  I'm somewhat surprised that these components sell at these prices.  I guess if there is no alternative, then you have to pay a premium price now.

I just checked the "Astrovision Bill Of Materials" that is dated 10-5-1981 for the cost of that Regulator Variable (ua78GU1C) that Matt bought for $35.  It cost $1.18 in 1981.  It is listed near the top of page 6, here:

https://ballyalley.com/documentation/Astrocade_Inc/pdf/Astrovision%20Bill%20Of%20Materials%20(10-5-1981).pdf

If you haven't seen this 12-page complete Bill of Materials that lists a breakdown of the cost to build the Bally Astrocade, then you should check it out and look it over.  The original source material was very light and hard to read. This is the best scan that could be made from it.  I find it somewhat amazing that we have this document to look at now at all.

Handwritten at the top of the first page of the BOM is that the total Astrocade system cost $125.  Sadly, by December of 1982, just a year or so later, these same Astrocades were being sold as surplus for $98 from places such as C.O.M.B.  Here is an example in an advertisement from the Minneapolis Star and Tribune:

https://ballyalley.com/ads_and_catalogs/ads_and_catalogs.html#COMBAstrocadeLiquidationAd

I think that this ad is from before the American videogame crash in 1983/1984.  During the "Crash," the Astrocade would sell new in the box for as low as $25 to the public in ads in newspapers.  I think they sold as low as about $50 in Montgomery Ward during this same period.

I was surprised at the cost of the custom chips in the Bill of Materials.  The prices for these were:

1) Address Chip - $9.10
2) I/O Chip - $9.10
3 Data Chip - $13.60

Also, the Z80 CPU (MK 3880 2 MHz) cost $8.00.

Needless to say, the Astrocade was not cheap.  I wonder what the cost was to build the Atari 2600 in 1981?

With such an expensive-to-build game system in 1981, I have to wonder if Astrocade, Inc., even if they had done everything right, and the systems weren't prone to failure, was there any hope that the Astrocade could survive in the marketplace at all at the time?

Adam
19151:
Certainly the 2600 didn't cost as much to build as a Bally astrocade. For one it uses a 6507 as a CPU which has less pins I believe then 6502 or 6809 or z80 processors and it's cheaper. The only other place I've ever seen 65-07's used to CPUs are in Atari smart disc drives.

Plus the Atari 2600 didn't have any RAM chips to worry about everything was done and what $128 bits of RAM on one of the internal chips or something like that. I don't know if you guys have ever read the book chasing the beam, but everything was done basically on the fly from ROM to screen.

It also only had the one custom chip the TIA, which probably wasn't that expensive for him to make.

19153:
Considering in 1981 the Atari VCS/2600 had Space Invaders, Asteroids, and
Missile Command preceding a whole stream of additional big names and
licenses, Mattel had the sports league licenses before getting third party
support and their own arcade and other licenses out in 1982, and the
ColecoVision was right around the corner with its own licensed games and
blockbuster pack-in for the time (not to mention the technical jump), it
was going to be extremely hard for Astrocade to remain competitive
regardless of what they did. Bally's own heavier hitter arcade games didn't
start to appear until 1981 and they already weren't involved in the system
by then for several years. It was probably a no-win situation by that point
because they couldn't compete on depth and breadth of library and,
especially in hindsight, there was no market for console-to-computer
expansions (not that they would have been able to afford to do that anyway).

    On Friday, April 1, 2022, 11:51:38 AM EDT, Adam Trionfo <ballyalley@hotmail.com> wrote:  
 
 Matt said:

"one regulator (UA78GUIC) [for that I must replace in the Astrocade] cost me $35! And one transistor (I don't remember which between TIP31 and TIP137) cost $15!"

I had no idea that some of the components in the Bally Arcade are so rare now.  I'm somewhat surprised that these components sell at these prices.  I guess if there is no alternative, then you have to pay a premium price now.

I just checked the "Astrovision Bill Of Materials" that is dated 10-5-1981 for the cost of that Regulator Variable (ua78GU1C) that Matt bought for $35.  It cost $1.18 in 1981.  It is listed near the top of page 6, here:

https://ballyalley.com/documentation/Astrocade_Inc/pdf/Astrovision%20Bill%20Of%20Materials%20(10-5-1981).pdf
If you haven't seen this 12-page complete Bill of Materials that lists a breakdown of the cost to build the Bally Astrocade, then you should check it out and look it over.  The original source material was very light and hard to read. This is the best scan that could be made from it.  I find it somewhat amazing that we have this document to look at now at all.

Handwritten at the top of the first page of the BOM is that the total Astrocade system cost $125.  Sadly, by December of 1982, just a year or so later, these same Astrocades were being sold as surplus for $98 from places such as C.O.M.B.  Here is an example in an advertisement from the Minneapolis Star and Tribune:

https://ballyalley.com/ads_and_catalogs/ads_and_catalogs.html#COMBAstrocadeLiquidationAd
I think that this ad is from before the American videogame crash in 1983/1984.  During the "Crash," the Astrocade would sell new in the box for as low as $25 to the public in ads in newspapers.  I think they sold as low as about $50 in Montgomery Ward during this same period.

I was surprised at the cost of the custom chips in the Bill of Materials.  The prices for these were:

1) Address Chip - $9.10
2) I/O Chip - $9.10
3 Data Chip - $13.60

Also, the Z80 CPU (MK 3880 2 MHz) cost $8.00.

Needless to say, the Astrocade was not cheap.  I wonder what the cost was to build the Atari 2600 in 1981?

With such an expensive-to-build game system in 1981, I have to wonder if Astrocade, Inc., even if they had done everything right, and the systems weren't prone to failure, was there any hope that the Astrocade could survive in the marketplace at all at the time?

Adam

Matt has a good idea with that Y-cable splitter, but it won't work with AstroBASIC.  He will need to find or construct a toggle switch so that there is a write-mode and a read-mode.  The toggle would be set to write for the :PRINT command and to read for the :INPUT command with AstroBASIC.

I built one of these toggle-switch boxes after reading the article in:

Steve Walters. "I-O Switch For New Bally BASIC Cartridge." ARCADIAN 4, no. 2 (Dec. 07, 1981): 16.

Here is a link to the article:

https://ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/arcadian_vol_4/arcadian_vol_4_issue_02.pdf#Page=4

These are really handy and if you plan to use AstroBASIC to write any software at all, then these are essential, else you'll be switching the cord in the AstroBASIC cart every time you load or save a program.

Adam

Yep, the Y adapter will be added into the Bally upgrade blog on Atari age.I just haven't had time really and then when I have I've been doing other things and haven't thought about it.

But, since it's become the immediate focus of this topic I will go ahead and talk about it a little bit. As you may have guessed at why adapter is the type that has the hollow hard plastic shell instead of being molded.

So since I was able to take it apart and do some modifications I decided I would much rather have an inline switch than an extra switch box. But there wasn't room enough for even the small micro switch I used to just cut a little rectangle in the case with the switch protruding.

So while sitting there pondering how I was going to attach the switch to this thing and not have to use something else, I was blankly staring at a couple of small sockets sitting on a breadboard in front of me.

And these sockets happen to have a small rectangular opening in the middle of them. Just about the size for a micro switch to slip in between. Of course I did have to shave down the inner sides of the socket some but was able to push the micro switch up in there.

I then removed all of the sockets pins and drilled the small hole through the middle of the y adapter case just big enough for a couple of small wires to fit through.

Then I soldered the wires to the switch and I grabbed my tube of trusty E6000 industrial strength adhesive and glued the socket to the side of the switch.

Then covering it all with electrical tape to make it look a little bit nicer for the meantime. I'm actually going to print out a little cover for it with my 3D printer eventually.


Even though I thought it would be kind of cool to have those vintage mini jack cables that are from the '60s or '70s themselves, I decided they just stick up a bit too much and I'm going to go ahead and use some modern ones that I have that have very tiny plugs on them and won't stick up nearly as high.

But, since it's become the immediate focus of this topic I will go ahead and talk about it a little bit. As you may have guessed at why adapter is the type that has the hollow hard plastic shell instead of being molded.

So since I was able to take it apart and do some modifications I decided I would much rather have an inline switch than an extra switch box. But there wasn't room enough for even the small micro switch I used to just cut a little rectangle in the case with the switch protruding.

So while sitting there pondering how I was going to attach the switch to this thing and not have to use something else, I was blankly staring at a couple of small sockets sitting on a breadboard in front of me.

And these sockets happen to have a small rectangular opening in the middle of them. Just about the size for a micro switch to slip in between. Of course I did have to shave down the inner sides of the socket some but was able to push the micro switch up in there.

I then removed all of the sockets pins and drilled the small hole through the middle of the y adapter case just big enough for a couple of small wires to fit through.

Then I soldered the wires to the switch and I grabbed my tube of trusty E6000 industrial strength adhesive and glued the socket to the side of the switch.

Then covering it all with electrical tape to make it look a little bit nicer for the meantime. I'm actually going to print out a little cover for it with my 3D printer eventually.


Even though I thought it would be kind of cool to have those vintage mini jack cables that are from the '60s or '70s themselves, I decided they just stick up a bit too much and I'm going to go ahead and use some modern ones that I have that have very tiny plugs on them and won't stick up nearly as high.

Welcome to the group, Iron Spyder.  I approved you this morning for this discussion group, Iron Spyder.  Why not tell us all a little bit about yourself.  How did you get introduced to the Astrocade?  Are you new to the system?

There aren't any available "mods" for the Astrocade; it's mostly a do-it-yourself affair.  Of course, there is no fan in the Astrocade, but people have added some small heat sinks to the custom chips.  Some people also remove the RF shielding (I have), but some people have somehow messed up their systems doing this mod, through static discharge, I guess.

There are some external add-ons, such as RAM and multicarts.  I'm sure people who sell these are here and can fill you in on the details.

If you have AstroBASIC, then you can load hundreds of BASIC programs.  It seems most people don't use their Astrocade in this way, preferring to use the cartridges, but there were not that many cartrs, so trying out some BASIC games can really expand the Astrocade's library.  Also, I love video art, and there is a lot of it available on the Astrocade.

I'm glad to hear that you use RF-out.  When used with a CRT TV, this is my favorite way to play old game systems.  The signal may have some interference, but that's okay with me.

Have fun with your Bally Arcade system!

Adam

I also have my classic console collection, which I will take some pictures of, if anyone is interested. That's all in an old-school wooden entertainment center on the opposite side of the room from my computer command center. with my 80's JVC Quadraphonic stereo system and my projector. All types of vintage media players too.

The Bally Arcade would have been set up among those other consoles instead of where it is, had it not been for the fact that I can DIY it into a real computer. So it becomes the third in my odd-ball trilogy of desktop vintage computers along with the Atari 1200XL and my Radio Shack TRS-80 Coco 2 (I also have an unfinished blog about upgrading the Coco 2, which has been put on hold since about November when I picked up where I had left off 2 years earlier restoring the Bally.

The 800CX is compatible with the 1200XL, so though I have four vintage computers it's still just a trilogy of different ones, covering the three leading CPU's of the golden age: Z80, 6502 and 6809 (though I upgraded to the compatible but better and faster 6309 in my Coco 2).
19192:
Well, Mister HR, I have that custom qwerty keyboard on order, and while waiting with anticipation I noticed the MLM keys are different from the Basic keys, so I'd have to have to sets of labels in different keys and I figured it would look awful. So it occurred to me that there just might be real key keypads that come with 24 keys. And I was right, so I decided to have qwerty and numerical keyboard/pad. I was right, but as you found, only one type is available, even if from multiple retailers, and yes, it is USB and did come with a USB cable.

But just like keyboard I'm waiting on, though it is kit and I will have to assemble even the keys, and the keypad is ready to use, they are both mechanical and I will be dis-assembling the USB keypad and turning it into a DIY kit. I will be hard-wiring my own matrix directly to the mechanical keys on both the keyboard and keypad. When I'm ready, I'll be removing the keypad from the case I made it, and tearing out the PCB in it and modifying it if I can, or making my own from scratch.

Both keyboard and keypad will be hard-wired to the Bally's on-board keypad, via the 10-pin "test" edge connector on my motherboard revision and the Bally won't know the difference between them and the on-board keypad. Just a simple direct wire matrix to both. I will be creating a simple wire matrix with open and closed contacts directly to the mechanical keys just like is done on the Bally keypad and it's contact switches under the keys. Very basic and simple stuff here, just a lot of wires and re-wiring to deal with.
19193: Here are a few photos of the dis-assembled keypad. I will be isolating the keys from most of the current motherboard by cutting traces like seen in the close-up of the keypad mobo. I will then be using some copper circuit maker tape, cut into thin strips, about 6-8 per the width of the tape as seen in the photo. I have to use the circuit maker tape because of the basically solid structure of the keypad, with "windows in the clear part to allow for the through-hole pins of the keys, which is the only areas I will be soldering. The circuit tape has conductive adhesive. And so I will create a new circuit over the old, matching the Bally's actual keypad circuit and the Bally won't know the difference...

My so-called "table" of projects exists in my mind and in my hobby room. Some of these project ideas will likely never materialize.

For example, on my table is an 8KB x 4 (32KB multi-cart) programming package, 3 of the programs which utilize an upgraded variation of AstroBasic's 2000 BAUD audio tape interface. The 4 programming package would include:

AstroBasic (4KB original low-res version)
Upgraded low-res Bit Fiddler's (BF) MLM
Hi-Res MLM
AstroBasicHR

AstroBasicHR would be an upgraded 4 color hi-res variation of AstroBasic with a user set up similar to the BF MLM. Remember, the hi-res mode utilizes 16KB of screen RAM. AstroBasicHR could require more than 8KB of ROM? Since there doesn't seem to be much of an interest in a modified for hi-res Astrocade and because I particularly have no interest programming in BASIC, AstroBasicHR would likely be replaced with something else, perhaps BalcheckHR.

Sorry, I do have a tendency at times to get carried away with myself. However, I do think the above example is a good project idea at least for my personal use.

Because I have already stripped down the keypad, I can provide you with a detailed matrix wiring description, if you need it. A photo or 2 of the underlying keypad matrix may not be beneficial.

Astrocade User Note
Keypad Strip Down Warning

MCM Design does not recommend stripping down the Astrocade's rectangular keypad, UNLESS the keypad matrix is in need of repair.

There are 6 separated copper overlays that rest on top of the embedded matrix wiring laid out on top of the 2 3/8 x 3 1/2" rectangular plastic matrix support. This is the support which slides into the keypad mounting. Each overlay lays loose and is mechanically connected ONLY at one point (at one underlying matrix line).

Care and patience is required when stripping down the keypad, so the loose, fragile overlays are not bent or their mechanical connections broken. However, It is possible to solder a broken connection.

The Astrocade 24 Button Keypad Matrix

By MCM Design
April 2022

This Doc serves as a dual intent providing info to help an Astrocade user who:

Wants to rewire an upgraded remote 24 key keyboard to be compatible as a substitute for the Astrocade built-in keypad or
Desires to strip down the keypad to repair a keypad matrix issue.

THE KEYPAD MATRIX PHYSICAL LAYOUT

The 10 keypad matrix lines soldered to the motherboard along with the keypad ROW and COLUMN pointers are all labeled on page 1 of MCMs Doc "Astrocade Keypad Repair" posted on the Bally Alley. Here's the link to the dock.

https://ballyalley.com/faqs/faqs.html#:~:text=Astrocade%20Keypad%20Repair.

All 10 keypad matrix lines soldered to the motherboard are routed to the top of the plastic rectangular keypad support, which slides into the keypad support mounting on top of the Astrocade motherboard.

The 10 lines are laid out and embedded into the plastic support and are parallel to each other. Six copper overlays rest on top of the 10 embedded matrix lines. Each overlay is connected ONLY at one point to a specific matrix ROW line. See the attached 3 photos.

The 6 overlays, from the rear to the front of the keypad support, are electrically connected to the specific matrix ROW line as indicated below.

Overlay         Connected To
Matrix Line

OVRLY 0         ROW 0
OVRLY 1         ROW 1
OVRLY 2         ROW 2
OVRLY 3         ROW 3
OVRLY 4         ROW 4
OVRLY 5         ROW 5

There are four 9mm in diameter copper ROW contacts on each overlay, which are centered below each of the respective 4 keypad ROW buttons. Each circular ROW contact flexes downward, when the keypad button is pushed, to make contact with its specific matrix COLUMN line.

ELECTRICAL KEYPAD BUTTON MATRIX CONNECTIONS

Below is an overview of each keypad button showing its ROW to COLUMN connection when the button is pushed down.

COL 3       COL 2       COL 1       COL 0

ROW 0          C              Up            Down         %

ROW 1         MR            MS            CH            Div

ROW 2          7                8                9              x

ROW 3          4                5                6              --

ROW 4          1                2                3              +

ROW 5         CE              0                 .              =

STRIPPING DOWN THE KEYPAD TO ACCESS ITS MATRIX FOR A REPAIR ISSUE

As indicated in the Doc mentioned above, the keypad can be checked for functionality using the lowest R x 1 range on an ohmmeter.

Attach a short wire with alligator clips to one test probe. Clip this lead to the ROW number you want to test, which will free you up to move the other test probe to a COLUMN number with one hand and press the respective ROW button with the other hand.

Ideally, you should be reading close to zero ohms when a button is pushed. Aged contacts will result in higher resistance readings. If no resistance (infinity) is indicated, double check your ohmmeter connections. No resistance indicates you might have an issue (break) in the keypad matrix.

It is possible to access the keypad matrix by slowly, gently peeling back the black/aluminum combo layers on top of the matrix.

Be careful not to bend the circular contacts on the copper overlays or break the single overlay connection to its ROW line.

It is possible to solder a broken ROW connection.

Once the keypad matrix is exposed, try your ohmmeter again to see if you can locate the keypad functional issue.

End Of Document
